text: Gangabal Lake, also known as Haramukh Ganga, is an alpine, high-altitude oligotrophic lake located at the foot of Mount Harmukh in the Ganderbal district of Jammu and Kashmir, India. It has a maximum length of 2.5 kilometres (1.6 mi) and a maximum width of 1 kilometre (0.62 mi). The lake is fed by precipitation, glaciers, and springs and supports various fish species, including brown trout. Water from Gangabal flows into Nundkol Lake and then into the Sind River via Wangath Nallah, and it is traditionally regarded as the source of the Sind River. The lake holds significant religious importance in Hinduism, being considered one of the abodes of Shiva and a sacred site for Hindu pilgrimage, where Kashmiri Hindus perform ancestral and death rites by immersing the ashes of the deceased. It is referenced in several ancient Hindu Sanskrit texts as Uttaramanasa and Uttara ganga (lit. 'northern Ganga'), and is mentioned in the Mahabharata as a pilgrimage site alongside Nandikunda (Nundkol) lake. The Vishnu Smriti identifies it as a place for performing Śrāddha, and it is also referenced in the Nilamata Purana and Rajatarangini. In 1519, approximately 10,000 Kashmiri Brahmins died during a pilgrimage to Gangabal while immersing ashes of those killed by Mir Shams-ud-Din Araqi on Ashura, possibly due to landslides and early snowstorms near Mahlish Meadow. British colonial-era authors such as Walter Roper Lawrence, Cecil Tyndale-Biscoe, and Francis Younghusband documented the lake and its religious significance. In 1943, Vikram Sarabhai and a team conducted cosmic ray measurements near the lake. Hindus regard Gangabal as a manifestation of the Ganga and the region as an abode of Shiva, with the lake considered equivalent to the Ganga and Haridwar for ancestral rites. The annual Harmukh-Gangabal Yatra begins from the 8th-century Wangath Temple complex at Naranag. The lake is also invoked during the Kaw Punim festival. It is traditionally recognized as the source of the Sind River. Access to the lake is via a 45-kilometer road from Srinagar to Ganderbal, followed by a 15-kilometer trek upslope, which can be completed on foot or by horseback, with Gujjar shepherds visible during the journey. An alternative 25-kilometer trek from Sonamarg passes through Vishansar Lake and crosses three mountain passes—Nichnai, Gadsar, and Zajibal—at an average elevation of 4,100 meters. The lake can also be reached via a trek from Bandipore through Arin or from Gurez via Tilel. The trek occurs in an alpine environment with meadows, Gujjar huts, and herds of sheep and goats, crossing two passes above 4,000 meters.
